taylor_all_songs |>
    filter(!is.na(album_name), !is.na(duration_ms)) |>
    mutate(minutes = duration_ms / 60000) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = minutes, y = album_name)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    labs(
    y = "Song length (minutes)",
    title = "Taylor Swift song length by album",
    caption = "Source: TidyTuesday 2023-10-17 (taylor R package)"
  )











Show code
taylor_all_songs |>
  drop_na(album_name, duration_ms) |>
  mutate(minutes = duration_ms / 60000) |>
  group_by(album_name) |>
  summarize(median_min = median(minutes), n_songs = n()) |>
  arrange(median_min)


# A tibble: 13 × 3
   album_name                          median_min n_songs
   <chr>                                    <dbl>   <int>
 1 The Taylor Swift Holiday Collection       3.27       6
 2 Lover                                     3.32      18
 3 Midnights                                 3.39      20
 4 Taylor Swift                              3.55      15
 5 reputation                                3.80      15
 6 1989                                      3.85      16
 7 folklore                                  3.9       17
 8 Red                                       3.98      22
 9 Red (Taylor's Version)                    4.03      30
10 Fearless (Taylor's Version)               4.03      26
11 Fearless                                  4.07      19
12 evermore                                  4.08      17
13 Speak Now                                 4.43      17


This boxplot shows the distribution of Taylor Swift’s song lengths in minutes for each album. Speak Now has the longest median song length of 4.43 minutes, while Taylor Swift Holiday Collection has the shortest median song lengh of 3.27. The biggest outlier is on Red (Taylor’s Version), at just over 10 minutes, which is the 10-minute version of “All Too Well.
Data source: TidyTuesday 2023-10-17: Taylor Swift songs
Original source: Thompson W (2026). taylor: Lyrics and Song Data for Taylor Swift’s Discography. R package version 4.0.0, https://taylor.wjakethompson.com.

Show code
main_cast <- c("Monica Geller", "Rachel Green", "Phoebe Buffay", "Chandler Bing", "Joey Tribbiani", "Ross Geller")

friends |>
  filter(speaker %in% main_cast) |>
  count(season, episode, speaker, name = "n_lines") |>
  left_join(friends_info, by = c("season", "episode")) |>
  filter(!is.na(imdb_rating)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n_lines, y = imdb_rating)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~speaker) +
  labs(
    title = "Friends: lines per episode vs. IMDb rating",
    x = "Lines spoken in the episode",
    y = "IMDb rating",
    caption = "Source: TidyTuesday 2020-09-08 (friends R package)"
  )


`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'











Show code
friends |>
  filter(speaker %in% main_cast) |>
  count(season, episode, speaker, name = "n_lines") |>
  left_join(friends_info, by = c("season", "episode")) |>
  filter(!is.na(imdb_rating)) |>
  group_by(speaker) |>
  summarize(correlation = cor(n_lines, imdb_rating))


# A tibble: 6 × 2
  speaker        correlation
  <chr>                <dbl>
1 Chandler Bing       0.0293
2 Joey Tribbiani      0.0433
3 Monica Geller       0.149 
4 Phoebe Buffay       0.0560
5 Rachel Green        0.0917
6 Ross Geller         0.237 


This plot shows how many lines each main character in Friends speak in an episode compared with that episode’s IMDb rating. Each point is equal to one episode. Ross shows the strongest positive relationship of 0.23, while Chandler has the lowest correlation of 0.02. For all the characters though, the trend line is nearly flat, which suggests the number of lines is not strongly related to rating. The points are widely spread around every line, so line count alone doesn’t explain much of the variation in ratings.
Data source: TidyTuesday 2020-09-08: Friends
Original source: Hvitfeldt E. friends: The Entire Transcript from Friends in Tidy Format. R package, https://github.com/EmilHvitfeldt/friends. The episode information came from Wikipedia and IMDb, and the transcripts come from the Emory NLP character-mining project.
